newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Assembly opens amid row over secretary-general.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Assembly opens amid row over secretary-general.

text.p: The 51st annual session of the General Assembly opens on Tuesday under a cloud of intrigue, with the United States vowing to block a second term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

The atmosphere will contrast sharply with the harmony prevailing at last year's 50th anniversary celebrations when Boutros-Ghali, whose five-year term expires at the end of this year, was hailed by more than 150 world leaders.
Fewer than 40 world leaders are expected this time, though scores of foreign ministers will, as usual, take part in the three-week general debate scheduled to begin on September 23.

President Bill Clinton addresses the Assembly on September 24, followed the same day by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, and in the afternoon by Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
The foreign ministers of Germany, China and France are listed to speak the following day.
The assembly this year will be presided over by Ismail Razali, 57, Malaysia's veteran U.N. envoy, who has shepherded a number of U.N. bodies through difficult negotiations.
The dispute over who should steer the world body into the 21st century is certain to be a prime topic of bickering and bargaining among the diplomats flocking to New York.

Although Boutros-Ghali has wide support among U.N. members, the Clinton administration insists it will not relent, even after the Nov. 5 U.S. elections, in its opposition to another term for the 74-year-old Egyptian. It says a new helmsman is needed to reform the world body whose perennial penury is, ironically, due in large measure to the U.S. failure to pay its $1 billion debt dues on time.

A secretary-general is appointed by the 185-member General Assembly on the recommendation of the 15-nation Security Council whose five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- each has a veto.
With Boutros-Ghali showing no sign of bowing out, the situation resembles an immovable object about to encounter an irresistible force.
Expected to be a pervasive feature of the session is the crisis sparked by the recent entry of Iraqi troops into Kurdish-inhabited northern Iraq for the first time since the end of the 1991 Gulf war.

Though not an issue for the Assembly -- and one on which the Security Council itself is divided -- the repercussions of Iraq's action and the U.S. response in firing cruise missiles is bound to preoccupy the visiting dignitaries.

Another issue of broad concern, though also not on the Assembly agenda, will be the year-end deadline for withdrawing the NATO-led peace keeping operation in Bosnia and the need to replace it, probably by a smaller more flexible force.

Lending an upbeat note to the start of the session will be the opening for signature of a Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty adopted by the Assembly earlier this month. Though endorsed by a huge majority, it is uncertain when the treaty might enter into force since that requires ratification by all 44 countries with a nuclear capability, and India, at least, has vowed not to do so in the foreseeable future.
The Middle East peace process is likely to come under sharper scrutiny in view of the slowing of negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians and a virtual standstill on the Israel-Syria track.

-- Cuba -- The United States will undergo its annual U.N. roasting over its economic sanctions against Cuba, on grounds that Washington is trying to impose its legislation on other countries. This line of attack will be sharpened this year because new U.S. curbs directed against Libya and Iran for alleged involvement in terrorism are regarded by many as another attempt to foist American policy on others.

-- Taiwan -- For the fourth time in as many years, a proposal to discuss U.N. membership for Taiwan is certain to be smothered in the Assembly's steering committee, again preventing its inscription on the agenda. Pressed by about a score of African, Caribbean and Central American countries, the initiative is fought tooth and nail by Beijing, which took over China's U.N. seat from Taiwan in 1971.

-- Council elections -- Elections to fill five Security Council seats which fall vacant at the end of the year may provide some suspense. Australia, Sweden and Portugal are all vying for places now filled by Italy and Germany, and India and Japan contesting a seat held by Indonesia. In the Latin American and Caribbean group, Costa Rica and Bolivia are both eyeing a seat being vacated by Honduras. Kenya is the only candidate for an African place occupied by Botswana.
